content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) represent approximately 40% of all hospital-acquired infections, and about 80% of these hospital-acquired UTIs are linked to the use of urinary catheters. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether specific antibiotic prophylaxis regimens are more effective than others in preventing UTIs, reducing complications, improving quality of life, and being cost-effective in adults undergoing short-term catheterization (up to 14 days). The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and other sources, up to October 31, 2012. They also reviewed reference lists of identified trials. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing antibiotic prophylaxis with no prophylaxis in adults with short-term catheterization. Data extraction was performed independently by multiple reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion. When data were incomplete, the authors of the trials were contacted for clarification. Six randomized controlled trials involving 789 participants met the inclusion criteria. All six studies compared the use of antibiotic prophylaxis to no prophylaxis. The studies generally had a low to unclear risk of bias, with similar interventions and outcome measures. The primary outcome, bacteriuria, was significantly less common in surgical patients receiving antibiotic prophylaxis compared to those who did not (risk ratio [RR] 0.20; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.13 to 0.31). However, two non-surgical studies could not be combined in a meta-analysis due to heterogeneity, and only one of these studies showed a significant reduction in bacteriuria (RR 0.19; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.37). Two trials involving surgical patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria (255 participants) compared different types of antibiotic prophylaxis but found no significant differences in bacteriuria rates between the antibiotic regimens. Another study with 78 participants compared the use of antibiotics only at the time of catheter insertion versus throughout the entire catheterization period. Administering antibiotics only at catheter insertion resulted in significantly fewer cases of bacteriuria compared to continuous prophylaxis (RR 0.29; 95% CI 0.09 to 0.91). Secondary outcomes included pyuria, which was reported in two surgical studies (255 participants). When the data were pooled, the prophylactic antibiotic group had significantly fewer cases of pyuria (RR 0.23; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.42). One study reported a significantly lower number of gram-negative bacterial isolates in urine samples collected just before catheter removal (RR 0.05; 95% CI 0.00 to 0.79) and six weeks after hospital discharge (RR 0.36; 95% CI 0.23 to 0.56). No gram-negative isolates were detected in the treatment group before catheter removal. Additionally, pooled data from two studies showed a significant reduction in febrile morbidity among patients receiving antibiotic prophylaxis (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.89). Although all studies assessed microorganisms isolated from urine specimens, the data were too heterogeneous to combine in a meta-analysis and were instead presented narratively. Other secondary outcomes, such as economic analyses, length of hospital stay, and quality of life, were not addressed in detail. In conclusion, the limited evidence suggests that prophylactic antibiotics reduce the incidence of bacteriuria, pyuria, febrile morbidity, and gram-negative bacterial isolates in surgical patients undergoing bladder drainage for at least 24 hours postoperatively. There is also some evidence that prophylactic antibiotics reduce bacteriuria in non-surgical patients. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and to evaluate other outcomes such as cost-effectiveness and quality of life.
